summary: CropCompass is a decision-support tool for farmers in the sugarcane region of Morelos, Mexico. It uses six years of NASA Earth observation data (2020–2025) to help farmers explore crop rotations that improve soil health and are more resilient to changing rain and temperature. A farmer picks a zone, their current crop, whether the plot is irrigated, and how much they care about water savings, soil health, income and climate fit. The app then does four things. It diagnoses the zone: rainy season, bare-soil periods seen from space, frost and heat risk, dry spells, and dry/normal/wet years. It forecasts rainfall and vegetation for the next year. It compares six or seven rotations, including the current one, with a score that can be traced back to its inputs and a “worked in X of 6 years” backtest. Finally, it explains in plain English or Spanish why each option is suggested, what evidence supports it, what the risks are, and what still needs local validation. The tool supports farmer judgment; it does not replace it.
details:
What it does

Farmers in the sugarcane region of Morelos, Mexico, are dealing with rain that is harder to predict, long dry seasons, and soil left bare for months between harvests. Choosing a new crop for a rotation is risky: a crop that improves the soil can still use too much water, miss the rainy season, or have no local buyer.

CropCompass is a decision-support tool that turns six years (2020–2025) of NASA Earth observation data into four answers a farmer or extension agent can act on:

  1. Zone diagnosis: when the rainy season starts and ends, when fields are bare (from satellite NDVI), which periods carry frost or heat risk, the longest dry spells inside the rainy season, and whether each year was dry, normal or wet.
  2. One-year forecast: rainfall and vegetation (NDVI) for the next 17 periods, with uncertainty bands and an honest comparison against a simple baseline.
  3. Rotation comparison: a 0–100 score for six or seven rotations, including the farmer’s current one. The score is split into climate fit, water saving, soil health and income, and weighted by the farmer’s own priorities. Each rotation is also re-tested against the real weather of every year from 2020 to 2025, and the app reports in which years it would have failed, which crop failed, and why.
  4. Plain-language explanation: for every rotation, why it was suggested, the numbers behind it, its benefits, its risks, and what information is still missing.

How it works

  • Data sources: rainfall comes from GPM IMERG and temperature from NASA POWER. Vegetation comes from MODIS NDVI, used for bare-soil detection.
  • Unit of analysis: each year is split into 17 fixed 21-day periods anchored to January 1. Monthly data are too coarse to see sowing windows and dry spells, and daily data are too noisy. Fixed periods make, for example, early June 2021 directly comparable with early June 2024.
    • Daily rainfall and temperature are summed or averaged per period.
    • The 16-day NDVI composites are cleaned of cloudy pixels, interpolated to daily values without bridging gaps longer than 32 days, and averaged per period.
    • The result is one integrated table of 306 rows (3 zones × 6 years × 17 periods).
  • Crop suitability: FAO EcoCrop-style fuzzy curves for temperature and rainfall over each crop’s cycle, plus a frost penalty. The weakest factor sets the suitability and is reported as the limiting factor.
  • Forecasting: a seasonal naive baseline, Prophet, and sliding-window Linear Regression and Random Forest models are compared on a strict temporal hold-out, with no information leakage. In all six zone/variable cases the best model beat the baseline, cutting forecast error by 16–38%.
  • Explanations: deterministic templates filled with computed numbers. Results are reproducible, and the English and Spanish versions always show the same figures.

Benefits

  • Shows when fields sit bare, which are the windows where cover crops or legumes could protect and enrich the soil.
  • Compares the current practice against alternatives on the same evidence: maize with common bean, sorghum with jack bean, peanut with sunn hemp, or a sugarcane renewal break.
  • A “Rainfed” switch shows where rainfall alone would limit each crop, which matters as water becomes scarcer.
  • Treats uncertainty as part of the answer: failed years, limiting factors, forecast error and information gaps are always shown.

Intended impact

We want small and medium farmers, and the agronomists who advise them, to have a free and understandable starting point for conversations about rotation. Moving even part of the land away from continuous monoculture and bare fallow could reduce erosion, add nitrogen and organic matter, break pest cycles and lower water demand. The design scales: adding a new zone only requires its coordinates and NASA data, and the crop parameters can be edited in the app.

Creativity

  • Fixed 21-day periods work as a common “language” between the satellite, the weather and crop calendars.
  • The backtest is told as a story (“worked in 5 of 6 years; failed in 2024, a wet year, because sorghum got too much rain”) instead of a single score.
  • Explainability is built into the design. No black box decides the ranking, so every number can be traced back to its data.
  • The interface is bilingual, with a guide mode that adds a short “how to read this” note to every tab for users without technical training.

Factors the team considered

  • Who will use it: farmers with little technical background. The app uses plain language, Spanish, a guide mode, and status shown with both icon and text, never color alone.
  • Water: irrigated versus rainfed scenarios, and a water criterion that counts a dry-season crop as extra demand.
    • NASA POWER’s grid cell for Cuautla sits about 800 m above the farmed valley, so temperatures there are likely about 4 °C too cold. The app shows a warning.
    • NDVI is sampled from a roughly 2 km window, not a single plot.
    • Six years is a short record.
  • Validation: crop parameters and candidate rotations are labeled as hypotheses everywhere. They must be checked with local agronomists and can be edited in the app.
  • Human judgment: the app repeats that it supports, and does not replace, the farmer and local experts.

Tools and technologies

  • Language: Python 3.11
  • Data and modeling: pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, Prophet (with CmdStan)
  • Interface and visualization: Streamlit, Plotly, pydeck (with an Esri World Imagery basemap)
  • Testing: pytest (107 tests)
  • Hardware: standard laptops, no GPU or paid services. The app runs locally or on Streamlit Community Cloud.

Use of AI

  • Inside the app: machine learning (Prophet, Random Forest and Linear Regression) forecasts rainfall and NDVI, and each model is validated against a baseline. The rotation ranking is deliberately rule-based, so every result can be explained and reproduced. No language model runs inside the app.
  • During development: Claude Code by Anthropic wrote the code, tests and documentation, working phase by phase from a plan written by the team. The team made the product decisions and approved each phase.
